## B8. Low Back: Non-specific LBP

> **Format note:** This protocol applies the standard Module 2.3 7-14-28 day phase framework to non-specific low back pain (NSLBP) — the most common musculoskeletal presentation in outpatient physiotherapy worldwide. Non-specific LBP is defined as pain in the lumbosacral region without a specific identifiable pathoanatomical cause (disc herniation, fracture, infection, malignancy, inflammatory arthritis, or radicular syndrome). It is a diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out red flags (B8.12) and specific pathology (B9-B12). The term "non-specific" does not mean "untreatable" — it means the precise tissue source cannot be confidently identified, but the condition remains highly responsive to an active, movement-based, education-led physiotherapy approach. This protocol is the foundation from which all other low back protocols (B9-B12) diverge once a specific pathoanatomical driver is identified.

### B8.1 Anatomy Link

The lumbar spine comprises five vertebrae (L1-L5), with the lumbosacral junction (L5-S1) as the most mobile and most commonly symptomatic segment. Non-specific LBP can arise from any of the following structures, often in combination:

- **Intervertebral discs:** the annulus fibrosus is innervated in its outer third; discogenic pain is typically deep, central, or paramedian, and aggravated by sustained loading (sitting, forward flexion) and relieved by positional change. Unlike lumbar disc herniation (B9), there is no radicular component — the pain remains axial.
- **Zygapophyseal (facet) joints:** paired synovial joints between adjacent lumbar vertebrae; facet-mediated pain is typically unilateral or paramedian, aggravated by extension, rotation, and rising from flexion, and relieved by flexion. Pain may refer to the buttock or posterior thigh but does not extend below the knee (that would suggest radiculopathy, B9).
- **Sacroiliac joint (SIJ):** pain localized to the posterior pelvis, aggravated by sitting, rising, and unilateral weight-bearing; managed separately when dominant (B11), but often co-present in NSLBP presentations.
- **Lumbar muscles and fascia:** the erector spinae, multifidus, quadratus lumborum, and thoracolumbar fascia — pain arises from sustained contraction, trigger points, fatigue, or reflex guarding in response to other lumbar pathologies. Multifidus atrophy and delayed activation are common motor-control findings in chronic NSLBP.
- **Ligaments:** the supraspinous, interspinous, and iliolumbar ligaments may be strained in acute flexion/rotation injuries.

> **Clinical Note:** The pathoanatomical source of NSLBP cannot be reliably identified in the majority of cases, and imaging findings (disc degeneration, facet arthropathy, mild disc bulges) correlate poorly with symptoms — they are equally common in asymptomatic individuals of the same age. This is the central paradox of NSLBP management: the pathology is real but the precise tissue driver is unknowable in most cases, so treatment targets function, movement, and pain modulation rather than tissue-specific repair. This is the single most important patient education point in this protocol.

### B8.2 Assessment Clues

Building on Module 1's standard assessment, with non-specific-LBP-specific additions:

| Finding | Typical Non-specific LBP pattern |
|---|---|
| Onset | Often insidious or related to a trivial mechanical trigger (e.g. "I bent over to pick something up" or "I slept awkwardly") rather than a high-force trauma — sudden onset with clear trauma should raise suspicion for fracture or disc herniation (B9/B12) |
| Location | Axial low back (between T12 and the gluteal folds), may refer to the buttock or posterior thigh, but does not radiate below the knee — this is the key discriminator from radiculopathy (B9). Pain may be central, paramedian, or unilateral |
| Pain behavior | Mechanical: provoked by sustained positions (prolonged sitting, standing, bending), specific movements (especially flexion, extension, or rotation), and relieved by changing position, walking, or lying down — this mechanical pattern is the defining feature and differentiates it from inflammatory (morning stiffness >1 hour, night pain) or systemic pathology |
| AROM | Restricted in one or more planes; pain-limited rather than weakness-limited; flexion, extension, and/or lateral flexion may be provocative; the most painful direction(s) guide treatment emphasis |
| PROM / passive segmental testing | Passive intervertebral motion (central and unilateral PA pressures) may reproduce familiar pain at specific levels or be diffusely restricted — but unlike B9/B10-B12, segmental findings are often non-specific and variable |
| Muscle testing | Lower extremity myotomes (L2-S1) are full and symmetrical — this is the key discriminator against radiculopathy (B9), where myotomal weakness is a hallmark. Hip and core musculature may be weak/deconditioned (not neurologically weak) contributing to the movement pattern |
| Neurological exam | Normal — no myotomal weakness, no dermatomal sensory loss, normal reflexes, negative straight leg raise (or mildly positive bilaterally, not unilateral radicular). This must be confirmed before committing to an NSLBP label (B8.3) |
| Special tests | SLR is negative (or only produces bilateral hamstring tightness, not radicular pain); slump test may be mildly positive bilaterally but not reproducing unilateral radicular symptoms; facet provocation tests (extension/rotation, unilateral PA pressures) may be positive; sacroiliac provocation tests may be positive (B11 if dominant) |
| Movement pattern | Observable movement dysfunctions — flexion-dominant pattern (pain provoked by flexion, relieved by extension), extension-dominant pattern (pain provoked by extension, relieved by flexion), or multidirectional pattern. This pattern guides the directional preference that drives exercise prescription (B8.7) |
| Psychosocial factors | Fear-avoidance beliefs, catastrophizing, kinesiophobia, and yellow flags (B8.12) are particularly relevant in NSLBP, more so than in many other musculoskeletal conditions — screen actively and address with education and graded exposure |

> **Clinical Note:** The single most important discriminator in this condition is a full neurological examination (Module 1.6). Any neurological deficit, any radiating pain below the knee, or a positive SLR reproducing radicular leg pain means you are not dealing with NSLBP — these patients belong to B9 (Sciatica/Disc Prolapse) or a neurological referral pathway, not this protocol. NSLBP is a diagnosis of exclusion, and the exclusion of radicular/neurological involvement is non-negotiable.

### B8.3 Differential Diagnosis

| Differential | Distinguishing feature against Non-specific LBP |
|---|---|
| Sciatica / Disc Prolapse (B9) | Positive SLR reproducing radicular leg pain; dermatomal sensory loss; myotomal weakness; reflex changes; pain radiates below the knee into the leg/foot |
| Facet Joint Syndrome (B10) | Pain reproduced/aggravated by extension and rotation; unilateral PA pressure at a specific level reproduces familiar pain; pain is more clearly segmental than diffuse NSLBP |
| SIJ Dysfunction (B11) | Positive SIJ provocation tests (≥3 of: thigh thrust, Gaenslen's, distraction, compression, sacral thrust); pain localized to the posterior pelvis, aggravated by sitting and rising |
| Lumbar Spondylosis/Spondylolisthesis (B12) | Typically older patients (>50) for spondylosis; younger patients for spondylolisthesis; X-ray shows degenerative changes, disc space narrowing, or listhesis; often a mixed mechanical/radicular presentation |
| Inflammatory Arthropathy (e.g. ankylosing spondylitis) | Marked morning stiffness (>1 hour, often >30 minutes), night pain unrelieved by position change, improvement with exercise, systemic symptoms, younger male patient, family history |
| Lumbar Myelopathy | Bilateral lower extremity paresthesia/weakness, gait disturbance, bowel/bladder involvement, UMN signs (hyperreflexia, clonus, positive Babinski) — these are red flags (B8.12) requiring immediate referral |
| Myofascial Pain | Pain is more regional than segmental; active trigger points in paraspinal muscles reproduce the patient's pain pattern on palpation; segmental mobility testing is relatively normal — this is often part of NSLBP, not a separate diagnosis, but treatment may emphasize dry needling/soft tissue work alongside exercise |
| Hip Pathology (e.g. OA, gluteal tendinopathy) | Pain localized to the groin, anterior thigh, or greater trochanter; hip ROM restriction (especially internal rotation), not reproduced by lumbar movements; FADIR/FABER tests positive |

### B8.4 Phase Goals (7-14-28 Day Framework)

| Phase | Typical window | Primary aim | Key metrics to track |
|---|---|---|---|
| Phase 1 — Acute/Protective | Day 1-7 | Reduce pain, reduce irritability, educate on staying active within pain limits (bed rest is actively discouraged), identify directional preference (which movements ease symptoms), establish activity modification | NPRS trend (rest and movement); ability to identify and modify provocative postures; identification of directional preference (flexion, extension, or sidelying); patient verbalizes "hurt does not equal harm" education |
| Phase 2 — Sub-acute/Restorative | Day 7-14 | Establish directional preference-based exercise, improve lumbar mobility and motor control, address postural dysfunction, begin core stabilization and graded activity | Reduced pain during movement; ability to perform directional preference exercise correctly; improved functional mobility; reduced fear-avoidance behaviors |
| Phase 3 — Remodeling/Functional | Day 14-28 | Build core and lumbopelvic endurance and strength, integrate into functional/occupational demands, return to full activity, address psychosocial barriers actively | Pain-free completion of previously provocative occupational/functional tasks; return to work/sport/activity at a meaningful level; patient demonstrates self-efficacy in managing symptoms; independent postural self-management |
| Phase 4 — Discharge/Maintenance | Beyond Day 28 (chronic/recurrent cases, or slow-responders) | Independent self-management, relapse-prevention education, ongoing conditioning, addressing yellow flags (B8.12) if present | Patient demonstrates independent home program; outcome measure (ODI or RMDQ) approaching normative score; patient has a clear, written flare-management plan |

> **Clinical Note:** The most important principle in NSLBP is that bed rest is actively harmful — patients should be advised to stay as active as possible within the limits of pain, modifying activities rather than ceasing them. Complete rest beyond the first 24-48 hours delays recovery, increases disability, and drives fear-avoidance behavior. This must be communicated explicitly and repeatedly.

### B8.5 Session Time-Block Application

| Phase | Opening electro (~10 min) | Manual therapy (~10-12 min) | Exercise (~15-20 min) | Closing electro (~10 min) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Phase 1 | Heat pack (if comfort improves mobility and is not contraindicated by acute inflammation); TENS for pain modulation if high irritability; avoid heat if there is acute inflammation/tenderness (use ice in the first 24-48 hours post-acute injury) | Gentle soft tissue release to lumbar paraspinal and gluteal muscles; Grade I-II oscillations to symptomatic segments in pain-free or minimally symptomatic position; avoid aggressive mobilization in the first session if very irritable; identify directional preference | Directional preference exercise (e.g. press-ups for extension preference, knee-to-chest for flexion preference) performed within pain limits; gentle lumbar mobility exercises in the preferred direction; walking as tolerated; postural/ergonomic education (workstation setup, sitting posture, lifting technique) | Ice (if acute/inflammatory) or TENS (if irritability remains) |
| Phase 2 | Heat pack before manual therapy/exercise (to relax guarding and improve tissue extensibility) | Progress to Grade III-IV mobilization to restricted segments (unilateral and central PA pressures) based on findings; MET for lumbar/hip tightness; soft tissue release to trigger points; SIJ mobilization if indicated (B11 considerations) | Directional preference exercise progressed in volume/intensity; core stabilization (e.g. abdominal bracing, dead bug, bird-dog); lumbar mobility in the preferred direction; hip mobility work (to address associated hip tightness) | Minimal; optional ice if exercise provoked soreness |
| Phase 3 | Minimal/optional; shift to exercise-dominant sessions | Maintenance mobilization only for residual restrictions; hands-on time shifts to guided exercise form, functional training, and active coaching | Progressive core and lumbopelvic strengthening; functional and occupational endurance training; sport-specific retraining; graded return to provocative activities; postural endurance work | Minimal; taper in favor of exercise-dominant care |

> **Clinical Note:** Directional preference assessment (finding the movement direction that centralizes or eases symptoms) is the single most useful clinical tool in this condition. Ask: "Which movement makes your pain better?" and "Which movement makes it worse?" The patient's preferred direction — typically flexion (e.g. lying on the side in a fetal position) or extension (e.g. lying prone) — guides Phase 1 exercise prescription. If no clear directional preference exists, use a neutral spine/activity-pacing approach (B8.7).

### B8.6 Manual Therapy Detail

Manual therapy has moderate evidence in NSLBP, particularly in the acute phase to facilitate pain relief and improve mobility, but should always be paired with active exercise:

- **Phase 1:** Maitland Grade I-II oscillatory mobilizations — central PA pressures, unilateral PA pressures — applied to the symptomatic segment(s) identified in assessment (if any). Technique: oscillate at 2-3 Hz, low amplitude at the onset of resistance (not at end-range), pain-relief/irritability-reduction grade. Soft tissue release to lumbar paraspinal muscles, quadratus lumborum, gluteal muscles, and piriformis (palpate for trigger points/tension; apply ischemic compression for 30-60 seconds to active trigger points if not too irritable — if very irritable, avoid deep pressure and use gentle sustained pressure instead). Do not perform high-velocity thrust manipulation on the first visit until the patient's irritability and suitability is fully assessed.
- **Phase 2:** Progress to Grade III-IV mobilizations — larger amplitude oscillations reaching into the tissue resistance/restriction (end-range, but not pushing into sharp pain). Apply unilateral PA pressures at the segment(s) most restricted (reduced mobility on passive segmental testing). MET for lumbar rotation and side-flexion restriction: contract-relax with gentle pre-positioning into restriction, 5-second hold, 30-50% effort, repeat 3-5 times with increasing pre-positioning. SIJ mobilization if SIJ dysfunction is identified as a significant contributor (cross-reference B11 for detailed technique).
- **Phase 3:** Manual therapy tapers to maintenance and residual restriction targeting; the therapist's hands-on time increasingly shifts to guiding exercise form, particularly reinforcing correct core activation and movement quality during functional exercises.

> **Clinical Note on Lumbar Mobilization Technique:** The most commonly restricted segment in NSLBP is L4-5 or L5-S1. Unilateral PA pressures are generally more specific for facet-mediated pain and more discriminating than central PA pressures — a positive unilateral PA finding at a specific level (reproducing familiar pain) should be treated with targeted mobilization at that level in preference to a more global approach. If no segmental provocation is found, use a more general lumbar mobilization approach.

### B8.7 Exercise Prescription Detail

Exercise for NSLBP has four priority categories: (1) directional preference and mobility exercises, (2) core and lumbopelvic stabilization, (3) hip and lower limb mobility (given the high prevalence of hip tightness co-present), and (4) functional and occupational endurance training.

| Phase | Exercise focus | Example progressions |
|---|---|---|
| Phase 1 | Directional preference exercise in the pain-easing direction; gentle pain-free mobility; walking as tolerated; postural and ergonomic education | Extension preference: prone press-ups (McKenzie extension) — start with lying prone, progress to prone press-ups with hips down, progress to standing extension; perform in sets of 5-10, several times daily. Flexion preference: knee-to-chest in supine (single then double), supine pelvic tilt, sidelying fetal position for symptom relief; progress to seated flexion. No clear preference: gentle lumbar mobility in all planes within pain limits (cat-camel, pelvic tilts, gentle rotation), activity pacing education |
| Phase 2 | Progress directional preference exercise volume; core stabilization training; hip mobility; graded functional activity | Extension preference progression: increase press-up range/reps, add standing extension with hands on low back, add lumbar extension in quadruped. Flexion preference progression: progress from supine to standing forward flexion, add seated flexion, include hanging/lying traction. Core stabilization: dead bug (arms/legs), bird-dog, side-lying plank (regressed to modified plank if needed), abdominal bracing during activities. Hip mobility: kneeling hip flexor stretch, supine glute stretch, standing hamstring stretch |
| Phase 3 | Progressive core and lumbopelvic strengthening; functional/occupational endurance training; sport-specific retraining | Core strengthening progression: full plank, side plank, dead bug with resistance, bird-dog with resistance, anti-rotation drills (Pallof press). Functional training: squat/lunge/deadlift patterns with postural cueing, loaded carrying (farmer's carry), lifting technique practice (moderate loads with perfect form). Endurance training: graded walking/hiking program, cycling (if extension-tolerated). Sport-specific work: retraining running mechanics, golf swing, tennis serve, or other sport-specific postures with core stabilization cueing |

- **Dosage principle for NSLBP:** Start with low volume (e.g. 5-10 reps, 2-3 sets, 2-3 times daily for mobility; 3-5 sets of 8-15 reps for strengthening) and progress based on symptom response. Exercise should produce a tolerable flare (≤3/10 pain that settles within an hour) — this is the "sweet spot" for recovery. Complete avoidance of movement-based pain delays adaptation.
- **Pain-monitoring rule for this condition:** "Hurt does not equal harm" — exercise may produce a transient increase in symptoms (a "good" pain that settles quickly), but sharp or worsening pain that persists >1 hour is a signal to reduce load/volume. Distinguish between (a) muscle soreness/movement discomfort, and (b) sharp/aggravating pain — the former is acceptable and expected; the latter requires modification.
- **Walking prescription:** Walking is the single most accessible and effective early intervention for NSLBP. Prescribe: start with 5-10 minutes, 2-3 times daily, progressing by 5 minutes every few days as tolerated, aiming for 30-45 minutes daily. Walking must be pain-monitored: if pain increases during walking, reduce duration or pace; if pain settles during walking, it's a good sign.

### B8.8 Electrotherapy Detail

- **TENS:** Indicated for symptomatic pain relief in Phase 1, particularly for patients with high irritability or those who are not yet engaging effectively with active exercises due to pain. Conventional TENS (high-frequency, 80-120 Hz, low-intensity) applied to the lumbar paraspinal region — teach the patient home-use TENS if night pain or prolonged sitting pain is a barrier to sleep/work function.
- **Heat pack:** Useful before manual therapy and exercise in Phase 1-2 to relax guarding and improve tissue extensibility — a routine precursor to lumbar mobilization and stretching. Avoid if there is acute inflammation/swelling (first 24-48 hours post-acute injury).
- **Therapeutic ultrasound:** Weak evidence for NSLBP specifically — may be used as an adjunct for pain relief and muscle relaxation if the clinic includes it, but never substitutes for manual therapy or exercise time.
- **IFT:** Adjunctive for pain relief; following the same adjunctive principle as other conditions — not a substitute for active care.
- **Laser/LLLT:** Some evidence for short-term pain relief in NSLBP, but current evidence does not support it as a primary driver of recovery — use only as an adjunct where it is available and the patient responds symptomatically.

> **Clinical Note:** The evidence consistently supports exercise as the primary treatment for NSLBP, with manual therapy as a useful adjunct. Electrotherapy is a distant third-line intervention that should be used sparingly and never as a substitute for the active components of care (exercise and education).

### B8.9 Acupuncture / Dry Needling Detail

- Indicated for myofascial trigger points in the lumbar paraspinal muscles (erector spinae, multifidus, quadratus lumborum), gluteal muscles (gluteus medius, gluteus minimus), and piriformis, which are common in NSLBP and contribute significantly to the pain and guarding pattern.
- Particularly useful for trigger points in the quadratus lumborum (often palpated laterally in the lumbar region) and gluteus medius (a common source of referral pain to the lateral hip and buttock) — these are clinically common and highly responsive to needling.
- Rationale: reducing myofascial guarding can improve pain-free lumbar mobility, reduce referral symptoms, and allow more effective manual therapy and exercise in the same or following session — consistent with Module 2.5's acupuncture principle of enabling primary interventions.
- Not indicated as a primary treatment for lumbar joint dysfunction — it addresses the muscular component only, which is often secondary; if segmental mobility testing demonstrates a clear joint source, joint mobilization must also be performed; dry needling alone is insufficient.
- (Full needle selection, depth, technique, and safety precautions for each lumbar/gluteal muscle will be detailed in Module 6: Acupuncture/Dry Needling Protocol Library.)

### B8.10 Contraindications and Precautions

- **Lumbar manipulation (high-velocity thrust):** This is a moderate-risk intervention with potential for serious complications (disc herniation aggravation, cauda equina, vertebral fracture in osteoporosis). At Relife, lumbar manipulation is performed only by clinicians specifically trained and certified in spinal manipulation technique, and only after a full pre-manipulative safety screen (red flags, B8.12, and imaging where indicated). For non-certified clinicians, use Maitland mobilizations (Grade I-IV) as the primary manual therapy technique and do not substitute with thrust manipulation.
- **Acute radiculopathy (B9) red flags** — if a patient develops neurological symptoms (radiating leg pain, paresthesia, weakness) at any point during care, they should be reclassified to B9 and managed according to that protocol, not continued under the NSLBP label.
- **Cauda equina red flags** — saddle anesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction, bilateral leg weakness, progressive neurological deficit — absolute contraindication to lumbar manual therapy; refer immediately for emergency assessment.
- **Osteoporosis** — use lower-grade mobilizations (Grade I-II) and avoid high-velocity thrust manipulation; patients with known osteoporosis and lumbar pain should be managed with exercise and low-intensity manual techniques only.
- **Vertebral fracture** — a history of significant trauma, prolonged steroid use, or osteoporosis with sudden-onset severe pain are red flags; imaging is warranted before manual therapy.
- **Inflammatory arthritis** (e.g. ankylosing spondylitis) — a relative contraindication to high-velocity lumbar manipulation; use only gentle, low-grade mobilization techniques and coordinate with the patient's rheumatologist if manipulation is considered.
- **No imaging for routine NSLBP** — the clinical guideline consensus is that imaging is not routinely indicated for NSLBP without red flags or failure to improve; avoid unnecessary imaging in the absence of clear indications.

### B8.11 Progression Criteria

**Progress to the next phase/loading level when:**
- Phase 1 → 2: NPRS at rest reduced to ≤3/10; directional preference identified; patient can correctly perform directional preference and basic mobility exercises without symptom reproduction; walking program established.
- Phase 2 → 3: Pain-free movement in the previously provocative direction improved; core stabilization exercises performed with good form; functional mobility improved (e.g. sitting >30 minutes without significant pain, standing >30 minutes without pain, bending to floor with minimal discomfort).
- Within Phase 3, progress load/complexity when current exercise load is tolerated with ≤3/10 exercise pain that settles within 1 hour, and no >24h flare.

**Regress or hold when:**
- Pain during exercise exceeds 3/10 or persists >1 hour post-exercise; or a >24h flare occurs (return to the prior tolerated load level).
- New neurological symptoms appear (radiating leg pain, paresthesia, weakness) — halt lumbar mobilization and re-classify toward B9/neurological referral immediately.
- Lumbar ROM worsens on reassessment — screen for a new aggravating factor or alternate diagnosis before continuing.
- Pain is centralizing toward the lower back (a good sign — reducing volume but not discontinuing).
- Pain is peripheralizing toward the leg (a bad sign — stop the provoking exercise and reassess).

### B8.12 Red Flags Specific to This Condition

In addition to the universal red flags (Module 1, 1.2):

| Red Flag Category | Specific Indicators | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Cauda Equina Syndrome | Saddle anesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction, bilateral leg weakness, progressive neurological deficit, perianal sensory loss | Immediate emergency referral — do not perform lumbar manual therapy |
| Vertebral Fracture | Significant trauma (MVC, fall from height), prolonged steroid use, age >70 with minor trauma, sudden severe pain, inability to weight-bear | Urgent imaging and orthopedic referral |
| Malignancy/Infection | Unexplained weight loss, history of malignancy, fever/chills, recent infection, night pain unrelieved by position, immunosuppression, IV drug use | Urgent medical referral for blood work and imaging |
| Inflammatory Arthropathy | Marked morning stiffness (>1 hour), night pain, improvement with exercise, multiple joint involvement, systemic symptoms (fatigue, fever, weight loss), elevated ESR/CRP | Rheumatology referral; avoid aggressive manual therapy until diagnosis clarified |
| Progressive Neurological Deficit | New or worsening weakness, sensory loss, or reflex changes — especially if bilateral or affecting bowel/bladder | Urgent neurological/orthopedic referral; do not continue conservative care |
| Cauda Equina-equivalent (Lumbar Myelopathy) | Bilateral lower extremity paresthesia/weakness, gait disturbance, bowel/bladder involvement, UMN signs (hyperreflexia, clonus, positive Babinski) | Immediate neurological referral; do not perform lumbar manual therapy |

**Yellow Flags (Psychosocial risk factors for chronicity)** — particularly important in NSLBP:

- Fear-avoidance beliefs: "Movement will damage my back", "I must not bend or lift"
- Catastrophizing: "My back is ruined", "I'll never get better"
- Low mood/depression
- Passive coping strategies: relying on passive modalities rather than active self-management
- Work-related factors: job dissatisfaction, manual work, lack of workplace accommodations
- Litigation/compensation claims
- Social support deficit

> **Clinical Note:** Yellow flags predict poor outcome more strongly than the severity of physical findings in NSLBP. Address them explicitly through education (challenging fear-avoidance beliefs), graded exposure (demonstrating that movement is safe), and cognitive-behavioral principles (reframing "hurt" as not necessarily "harm"). If yellow flags are prominent, consider a psychologically-informed physiotherapy approach or referral to a clinical psychologist.

### B8.13 Home Exercise Program

| Phase | Home program emphasis | Example content |
|---|---|---|
| Phase 1 | Directional preference exercise; gentle pain-free movement; walking as tolerated; postural/ergonomic self-correction | Extension preference: prone press-ups 5-10 reps, 3-5 times daily; standing extension; avoid prolonged sitting. Flexion preference: knee-to-chest 5-10 reps, 3-5 times daily; supine pelvic tilt; avoid prolonged standing. No clear preference: gentle cat-camel, pelvic tilts, walking; avoid sustained positions. Ergonomic/workstation check; "take a break every 30 minutes" guidance; activity pacing |
| Phase 2 | Structured daily directional preference program; core stabilization; hip mobility; graded functional activity | Extension preference progression: press-ups with increased range/reps, standing extension. Flexion preference progression: standing forward flexion, seated flexion. Core stabilization: dead bug, bird-dog, side-lying plank (modified), abdominal bracing during daily activities. Hip mobility: kneeling hip flexor stretch, supine glute stretch, standing hamstring stretch. Walking progression: increase by 5 minutes every few days |
| Phase 3 | Progressive home strengthening program; functional and occupational retraining; long-term relapse prevention | Core progression: full plank, side plank, Pallof press (if band available). Functional training: squat/lunge/deadlift patterns with form cueing, loaded carrying. Endurance training: graded walking/hiking program. Sport-specific drills: running mechanics, golf swing, tennis serve with core cueing |

- **Most important patient education message for this condition:** "Hurt does not mean harm. Your back is strong. Moving, even when it hurts a little, will help you recover faster than resting. The worst thing you can do is stop moving completely." Frame this explicitly and repeatedly.
- **Flare management plan:** provide every patient with a written plan for managing future flares: (1) stay active and continue walking; (2) resume directional preference exercises; (3) avoid prolonged sitting or standing; (4) modify lifting technique; (5) use heat/ice for comfort; (6) if symptoms persist >48 hours or new neurological symptoms appear, contact the clinic.
- Address workplace ergonomics explicitly: desk setup, chair adjustment, monitor height, lumbar support, regular breaks, lifting technique. Many NSLBP patients are desk workers; an optimized workstation is a key relapse prevention strategy.
- Address sleep posture: sidelying with a pillow between knees is generally best for the lumbar spine; supine with a pillow under the knees is also good; avoid prolonged prone lying.
- Address lifting technique: teach "sit-to-stand" lifting (hinge at the hips, keep the back straight, engage the core, keep the load close to the body) — practice it with light loads in the clinic so the patient can do it safely at home.
- (Full templated home program handouts will be built in Module 10: Home Exercise Program Templates.)

### B8.14 Evidence Grade Summary

| Intervention | Evidence Level | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Exercise therapy (any form) | High | Strongest evidence for NSLBP — exercise is the primary treatment; type of exercise matters less than adherence and active participation |
| Manual therapy (mobilization, manipulation) + exercise combined | Moderate-High | Combined approach more effective than exercise alone; manual therapy alone is less effective without exercise |
| Education and advice (staying active, "hurt ≠ harm") | Moderate-High | Strong evidence for addressing fear-avoidance; essential component of care |
| Walking program | Moderate | Direct evidence; highly accessible and effective for most patients |
| Cognitive-behavioral / psychologically-informed approaches | Moderate-High | For patients with prominent yellow flags; may be essential for some patients |
| TENS | Low-Moderate | Symptomatic adjunct for pain modulation, especially for sleep disruption |
| Heat therapy | Low-Moderate | Symptomatic/comfort only; useful for muscle relaxation and comfort |
| Therapeutic ultrasound / IFT / laser | Low | Weak adjunctive evidence; never a substitute for exercise or education |
| Lumbar traction | Low (for this condition specifically) | Weak evidence for NSLBP; unlike B9 (radiculopathy), traction is not a standard component here |
| Dry needling (secondary myofascial guarding) | Low-Moderate | Adjunct only; addresses muscular component, not the primary NSLBP driver |
| Bed rest | Harmful | Active rest (staying active within pain limits) is recommended; bed rest beyond 1-2 days delays recovery |

### B8.15 Outcome Measures & Cutoffs

| Measure | What it captures | Clinically meaningful change (MCID) | When to administer |
|---|---|---|---|
| ODI (Oswestry Disability Index) | LBP-specific disability | ~10-12 points | Baseline, then every reassessment point |
| RMDQ (Roland-Morris Disability Questionnaire) | LBP-specific disability | ~3-5 points | Baseline, then every reassessment point |
| PSFS (Patient-Specific Functional Scale) | Patient-defined functional goals | ~2 points | Baseline, then every reassessment point |
| NPRS (rest and movement) | Pain intensity | ~2 points | Every session |
| STarT Back Screening Tool | Risk stratification for chronicity | Determines treatment intensity (low/medium/high), not a change-score measure | Baseline — strongly recommended for all NSLBP patients |

> **Clinical Note:** The STarT Back Screening Tool is a 9-item questionnaire that stratifies patients into low, medium, or high risk for persistent disability. It should be administered at baseline for all NSLBP patients. Low-risk patients can be managed with a simple directional-preference exercise program and education; medium-risk patients benefit from a more structured exercise and manual therapy program; high-risk patients require psychologically-informed physiotherapy (addressing yellow flags) and may benefit from a multidisciplinary approach.

### B8.16 AI Condition Card (RAG Metadata)

- **Condition:** Non-specific Low Back Pain (NSLBP)
- **Framework:** Standard 7-14-28 day phase framework; directional preference guides exercise prescription; yellow flags are actively screened
- **Key Symptoms:** axial lumbar pain, mechanical pattern (movement/posture-provoked, relieved by position change), normal neurological exam, no radiating pain below the knee
- **Red Flags:** cauda equina (saddle anesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction), fracture (significant trauma, osteoporosis, steroid use), malignancy/infection (weight loss, fever, night pain, history of malignancy), progressive neurological deficit, inflammatory arthropathy (prolonged morning stiffness >1 hour), myelopathy (bilateral/UMN signs)
- **Yellow Flags (psychosocial):** fear-avoidance beliefs, catastrophizing, low mood, passive coping, work dissatisfaction, litigation
- **Primary Treatment:** exercise therapy (directional preference, core stabilization, functional training), education and advice (staying active, "hurt ≠ harm"), manual therapy as an adjunct
- **Home Exercise Summary:** directional preference exercises and gentle mobility (Phase 1) → structured core stabilization and mobility (Phase 2) → progressive functional and occupational strengthening (Phase 3)
- **Typical Duration:** follows 7-14-28 day phase framework; most acute NSLBP improves within 4-6 weeks; chronic/recurrent cases benefit from an ongoing maintenance relationship and yellow flag management

*End of B8. Next in the tracker's work order: B9 — Low Back: Sciatica / Disc Prolapse.*

## B9. Low Back: Sciatica / Disc Prolapse

> **Format note:** This protocol applies the standard Module 2.3 7-14-28 day phase framework to lumbar radiculopathy secondary to disc herniation/prolapse — one of the most common and disabling low back conditions seen in outpatient physiotherapy. Sciatica is defined as pain radiating from the low back into the leg in a dermatomal pattern, with or without neurological deficit, caused by compression or chemical irritation of a lumbar or sacral nerve root, most commonly from a herniated intervertebral disc. This protocol covers the full spectrum from acute, highly irritable radiculopathy through to resolution, with explicit emphasis on centralization/peripheralization monitoring, neurological safety, and when to escalate for surgical referral.

### B9.1 Anatomy Link

The intervertebral disc comprises a central nucleus pulposus (gelatinous, high-water-content core) and a surrounding annulus fibrosus (concentric collagenous rings). Disc herniation occurs when nuclear material protrudes through a tear in the annulus, compressing or chemically irritating the adjacent nerve root.

- Lumbar disc herniation is most common at L4-L5 and L5-S1 — these segments bear the greatest load and have the most motion, making them vulnerable to annular tears.
- **Herniation types:**
  - **Protrusion:** the nucleus bulges but remains contained within the annulus — the most common type; often responds well to conservative care.
  - **Extrusion:** the nucleus breaks through the annulus but remains connected to the disc space — more likely to cause significant nerve root compression.
  - **Sequestration:** nuclear material separates from the disc space entirely and migrates — can produce dramatic symptoms, often with a self-limiting inflammatory phase, but may require surgical intervention if neurological compromise is significant.
- **Nerve root anatomy:**
  - **L4** nerve root exits at L4-L5 foramen; compression produces pain/dysfunction in the L4 dermatome (anterior thigh, medial lower leg), weakness in quadriceps (knee extension), and diminished patellar reflex.
  - **L5** nerve root exits at L5-S1 foramen; compression produces pain/dysfunction in the L5 dermatome (lateral leg, dorsum of foot, great toe), weakness in tibialis anterior (foot drop/weak ankle dorsiflexion) and extensor hallucis longus (great toe extension); no reliably testable reflex change — L5 radiculopathy is primarily identified by weakness and sensory loss.
  - **S1** nerve root exits at S1 foramen; compression produces pain/dysfunction in the S1 dermatome (posterior leg, lateral foot, sole), weakness in gastrocnemius/soleus (weak ankle plantarflexion), and diminished or absent Achilles reflex.
- **Mechanisms of pain:** the herniated disc produces symptoms through two mechanisms: (a) mechanical compression of the nerve root (stenosis of the foramen), and (b) chemical irritation from inflammatory mediators (phospholipase A2, prostaglandins, cytokines) released from the nucleus pulposus — this chemical component explains why radicular pain often improves with anti-inflammatory medical management and why the early phase may be more irritable than purely mechanical models predict.
- **Natural history:** the majority of lumbar disc herniations (roughly 80-90%) improve with conservative management within 6-12 weeks, even with significant radicular symptoms — this favorable natural history is the foundation of the physiotherapy approach, but it must be balanced against careful neurological monitoring for the minority that require surgical intervention.

> **Clinical Note:** The single most important anatomical distinction in this condition is between radiculopathy (neurological involvement — weakness, sensory loss, reflex change) and referred leg pain (pain that radiates from the back into the leg but is not associated with nerve root compression). This distinction is made clinically by the neurological exam (Module 1.6) — not by imaging alone. Many patients with imaging-confirmed disc herniations have no neurological deficits and are managed as B8 (NSLBP) with directional preference exercise, not as B9.

### B9.2 Assessment Clues

Building on Module 1's standard assessment and B8's low back findings, with radiculopathy-specific additions:

| Finding | Typical Sciatica / Disc Prolapse pattern |
|---|---|
| Onset | Often acute or subacute, frequently following a flexion or flexion-rotation injury (e.g. "I bent over to pick something up", "I twisted while lifting", "I sneezed and it went"), but may be insidious; can follow a prodromal period of low back pain before the leg symptoms develop |
| Location | Axial low back pain (may be present or absent) with pain radiating into the buttock and down the leg, typically below the knee, in a dermatomal pattern (L4, L5, or S1 distribution) — this is the key discriminator from B8 |
| Pain behavior | Often worsened by sustained sitting, forward flexion, coughing/sneezing/Valsalva (increases intradiscal pressure), and relieved by lying down, sidelying with a pillow between knees, or walking (some patients find walking eases symptoms; others find it aggravates — monitor this individually) |
| AROM | Restricted, especially forward flexion and ipsilateral side-flexion (increases disc pressure and radicular symptoms); extension may be limited and may peripheralize symptoms in some patients — the directional preference assessment (B9.7) is critical here |
| Straight Leg Raise (SLR) | Positive: reproduction of radicular leg pain (not just hamstring tightness) at <60° of hip flexion with the knee extended — the classic test for L5/S1 nerve root irritation. The contralateral SLR (raising the unaffected leg reproduces symptoms in the affected leg) is a more specific finding, suggesting a large central/paracentral disc herniation |
| Slump Test | Positive: reproduction of radicular leg symptoms when the patient is in a slumped sitting position with chin-to-chest, knee extension, and ankle dorsiflexion — a neurodynamic test that adds tension to the entire neural axis and can be more sensitive than SLR alone |
| Muscle testing | Myotomal weakness may be present corresponding to the affected level(s): L4 → quadriceps (knee extension), L5 → tibialis anterior (ankle dorsiflexion) and extensor hallucis longus (great toe extension), S1 → gastrocnemius/soleus (ankle plantarflexion) — graded formally (0-5 MMT) |
| Sensory testing | Dermatomal sensory change (hypoesthesia, paresthesia, or hyperalgesia) corresponding to the affected root: L4 → anterior thigh/medial lower leg, L5 → lateral leg/dorsum of foot, S1 → posterior leg/lateral foot/soles |
| Reflexes | Diminished or absent reflex corresponding to the level: L4 → patellar reflex diminished, L5 → no reliable reflex change, S1 → Achilles reflex diminished or absent |
| Centralization / Peripheralization | The most important dynamic assessment for this condition: does a movement or position cause the leg symptoms to move toward the spine (centralization — favorable sign) or further into the leg (peripheralization — unfavorable sign)? Centralization predicts good response to directional preference exercise; persistent peripheralization suggests a more irritable or structurally significant lesion |
| Functional impact | Gait disturbance (antalgic gait, foot drop if L5 significant), difficulty sitting, difficulty with transfers (getting in/out of a car, standing from sitting), sleep disruption from radicular pain, work/occupational limitation |

> **Clinical Note:** The centralization phenomenon (McKenzie) is the single most useful clinical predictor in this condition. If a movement (typically repeated extension, or sometimes repeated flexion) causes the leg symptoms to move proximally toward the low back — even if the back pain temporarily increases — this is a highly favorable sign and that movement should be incorporated as a primary exercise. If symptoms move distally (peripheralize) with a movement, that movement should be avoided. Document centralization/peripheralization direction at every visit.

### B9.3 Differential Diagnosis

| Differential | Distinguishing feature against Sciatica / Disc Prolapse |
|---|---|
| Non-specific LBP (B8) | No radiating leg pain below the knee; negative SLR; no myotomal weakness, dermatomal sensory loss, or reflex changes; pain is purely axial |
| Facet Joint Syndrome (B10) | Pain reproduced/aggravated by extension and rotation, not by flexion; pain typically remains above the knee, does not follow a dermatomal pattern; SLR is negative; no neurological deficit |
| SIJ Dysfunction (B11) | Pain localized to the posterior pelvis, aggravated by sitting and unilateral weight-bearing; positive SIJ provocation tests (≥3 of: thigh thrust, Gaenslen's, distraction, compression, sacral thrust); SLR is negative or only produces SIJ pain, not radicular leg pain |
| Lumbar Spondylosis/Spondylolisthesis (B12) | Typically older patients (>50) for spondylosis; X-ray shows degenerative changes, disc space narrowing, or listhesis; may co-exist with or cause radiculopathy from foraminal stenosis — B12 and B9 are frequently co-diagnosed rather than mutually exclusive |
| Neurogenic Claudication (Spinal Stenosis) | Bilateral or alternating leg symptoms (usually buttock/thigh, sometimes calf), precipitated by walking/standing, relieved by sitting/forward flexion; often older patients with MRI-confirmed central canal stenosis; SLR is typically negative; normal neurological exam at rest |
| Vascular Claudication (Peripheral Arterial Disease) | Leg pain/cramping with walking, relieved by rest (but requires standing rest, not just sitting); absent/reduced peripheral pulses, skin changes; risk factors for atherosclerosis (smoking, diabetes, hypertension) |
| Piriformis Syndrome | Buttock pain aggravated by sitting, deep palpation over the piriformis reproduces pain; SLR may be positive but pain is localized to the buttock, not radicular in a dermatomal pattern; no neurological deficit |
| Hip Pathology (OA, labral tear) | Pain localized to the groin, anterior thigh, or lateral hip; hip ROM restriction (especially internal rotation) is the key discriminator; SLR is negative or only produces hip pain, not radicular leg pain; FADIR/FABER tests positive |
| Cauda Equina Syndrome | Saddle anesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction, bilateral leg weakness, progressive neurological deficit — this is an urgent surgical emergency (B9.12) and requires immediate referral, not conservative management |

> **Clinical Note:** A positive SLR and a well-defined dermatomal pain pattern are the two most reliable clinical discriminators of discogenic sciatica from other low back conditions. However, absence of SLR positivity does not rule out a disc herniation (particularly small, lateral herniations may produce radicular pain without a positive SLR, or the patient may be very irritable and you cannot fully perform the test). Use the cluster of SLR, slump test, neurological exam, and centralization pattern to support the diagnosis.

### B9.4 Phase Goals (7-14-28 Day Framework)

| Phase | Typical window | Primary aim | Key metrics to track |
|---|---|---|---|
| Phase 1 — Acute/Protective | Day 1-7 | Reduce nerve root irritability and pain; identify symptom-easing positions and directional preference; educate on staying active within pain limits (relative rest, not complete bed rest); monitor neurological status closely for progression | NPRS trend for both back and leg pain tracked separately; direction of centralization/peripheralization; stability or improvement of neurological exam (no new weakness, sensory loss, or reflex change); ability to identify and use symptom-easing positions |
| Phase 2 — Sub-acute/Restorative | Day 7-14 | Progress directional preference exercise to centralize symptoms; reduce radicular pain intensity; begin gentle neurodynamic mobilization and core stabilization; monitor for continued centralization | Symptom centralization (leg symptoms retreating toward the low back); improving myotomal strength (if weakness was present); reduced pain during sitting; improved functional mobility (sitting tolerance, transfers) |
| Phase 3 — Remodeling/Functional | Day 14-28 | Restore functional lumbar mobility and strength; consolidate centralization; progress core and lumbopelvic strengthening; graded return to occupational/functional demands; address psychosocial barriers (fear-avoidance beliefs) | Resolution or substantial improvement of radicular symptoms; myotomal strength approaching full; return to functional tasks (sitting >30 minutes, standing, bending, lifting light loads) without symptom provocation; independent home program management |
| Phase 4 — Discharge/Maintenance | Beyond Day 28 (slow-responders, those with chronic radicular symptoms, or those awaiting surgical opinion) | Independent self-management, long-term postural and ergonomic strategy, relapse-prevention education; if no meaningful improvement by Day 28, escalate for imaging/surgical consult per B9.12 | Patient demonstrates independent home program and understands flare management; ODI approaching normative score; if plateaued or worsened, referral pathway initiated |

- **Time windows:** the acute radicular phase is often the most painful and disabling; many patients experience significant improvement within 7-14 days of starting physiotherapy. However, complete resolution of radicular symptoms may take 4-8 weeks or longer — set expectations accordingly with the patient (B9.13).
- **Neurological monitoring:** MMT, sensation, and reflexes must be re-checked at every visit until the radicular component is stable or improving — any worsening of neurological findings is a red flag (B9.12).

### B9.5 Session Time-Block Application

Applying the Module 2.4 template to sciatica/disc prolapse, weighted by phase:

| Phase | Opening electro (~10 min) | Manual therapy (~10-12 min) | Exercise (~15-20 min) | Closing electro (~10 min) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Phase 1 | Heat pack only if comfort improves mobility and is not contraindicated (avoid if the patient is highly irritable and heat worsens symptoms); TENS for symptomatic pain relief, especially for leg pain; ice if acute inflammatory component is prominent | Gentle soft tissue release to lumbar paraspinal and gluteal muscles for secondary guarding; avoid aggressive joint mobilization in the first session if very irritable; central PA pressures Grade I-II if well tolerated (some patients find this aggravates radicular symptoms — discontinue if so); focus on identifying the patient's symptom-easing position and directional preference | Directional preference assessment: repeated extension in lying (McKenzie prone press-ups) or repeated flexion (if extension peripheralizes), performed gently and monitored for centralization; if a directional preference is identified, prescribe it as the primary home exercise; positioning education (symptom-easing postures: sidelying fetal position, supine with knees bent, prone if extension-easing); gentle walking as tolerated | Ice (if acute/inflammatory) or TENS (if irritability remains) |
| Phase 2 | Heat pack before manual therapy/exercise if tolerated and not aggravating symptoms; TENS for pain modulation if still needed | Continue gentle mobilization (Grade I-II) to adjacent non-symptomatic segments if it provides relief; traction (manual or mechanical) trial if it reduces radicular symptoms — continue only if reproducible benefit is demonstrated; soft tissue work for secondary guarding; avoid any mobilization that peripheralizes symptoms | Progress directional preference exercise in volume/intensity (e.g. increase number of press-ups or knee-to-chest repetitions); introduce gentle neurodynamic mobilization (sliders, not tensioners) if tolerated; begin core stabilization (dead bug, bird-dog, but avoiding provocative flexion if it peripheralizes); gentle lumbar mobility in symptom-easing direction | Minimal; optional ice or TENS if provoked |
| Phase 3 | Minimal/optional; shift to exercise-dominant sessions | Maintenance mobilization as needed; traction if still clearly beneficial; manual therapy time shifts to guided exercise form and active coaching | Progressive core and lumbopelvic strengthening; neurodynamic mobility (sliders → tensioners as tolerated); functional training (squat, lift, carry with postural cueing); graded return to provocative activities (sitting, bending, lifting) | Minimal; taper in favor of exercise-dominant care |

> **Clinical Note on Traction:** Mechanical lumbar traction has moderate evidence specifically for radiculopathy, unlike for B8's non-specific LBP. Trial it in Phase 1-2 in a symptom-easing position (often slight flexion) and continue only if it produces a clear, reproducible reduction in leg symptoms during or immediately after the session. If it has no effect or worsens symptoms, discontinue and do not repeat.

### B9.6 Manual Therapy Detail

- **Phase 1:** Manual therapy in the acute radicular phase is gentle and conservative, prioritizing symptom identification (directional preference) over aggressive mobilization. Grade I-II central PA pressures at the symptomatic segment (L4-5 or L5-S1) only if they do not reproduce radicular symptoms — if even gentle PA pressures worsen leg pain, avoid them entirely and focus on exercise/positioning. Soft tissue release to lumbar paraspinal, quadratus lumborum, gluteal, and piriformis muscles for secondary guarding (these muscles often become tight and painful as a compensatory response to radicular pain). Do not perform high-velocity thrust manipulation or aggressive Grade III-IV mobilizations in the acute phase — this can aggravate the herniation and worsen radicular symptoms.
- **Phase 2:** If radicular irritability has settled (symptoms centralizing, pain reducing), progress to Grade III mobilizations, but only in directions that centralize symptoms (typically extension, but flexion in a subset of patients). Apply central and unilateral PA pressures to the symptomatic segment(s) with a carefully monitored symptom response — if a mobilization peripheralizes symptoms, discontinue and revert to the prior grade. Continue soft tissue work for secondary guarding. Trial traction (manual or mechanical) if not already done in Phase 1.
- **Phase 3:** Manual therapy tapers to maintenance; hands-on time shifts to guiding exercise form and neurodynamic technique. If residual mobility restriction persists and is not provoking radicular symptoms, progressive mobilization to end-range can be considered, but always with symptom monitoring.

> **Clinical Note:** The single most important manual therapy rule in this condition is: never push into pain that reproduces or worsens radicular symptoms. Unlike B8 (NSLBP), where movement into pain is acceptable and even desirable ("hurt does not mean harm"), in discogenic radiculopathy, peripheralization of symptoms is a clear negative signal and should be avoided. This is the central manual-therapy distinction between B8 and B9.

### B9.7 Exercise Prescription Detail

Exercise for discogenic sciatica is directional preference-centered, with the same three phases as B8 but with radiculopathy-specific modifications:

| Phase | Exercise focus | Example progressions |
|---|---|---|
| Phase 1 | Directional preference assessment and exercise in the pain-easing/centralizing direction; gentle pain-free mobility; walking as tolerated; positioning education | Extension preference (most common): prone lying (start with 5-10 minutes if tolerated), progress to prone press-ups (McKenzie extension) — start with elbows under shoulders, lift upper body while keeping hips down, perform in sets of 5-10 repetitions, several times daily, monitoring for centralization; progress to standing extension. Flexion preference (less common, but important in some patients): knee-to-chest in supine (single then double), supine pelvic tilt, sidelying fetal position; progress to seated flexion. No clear preference: gentle lumbar mobility in all planes within pain limits (cat-camel, pelvic tilts), but avoid directions that peripheralize. Walking as tolerated (some patients find walking eases symptoms; others find it aggravates — monitor carefully) |
| Phase 2 | Progress directional preference exercise volume/intensity; introduce gentle neurodynamic mobilization (sliders); core stabilization; gradual return to functional activity | Extension preference progression: increase press-up range/reps, add standing extension, add lumbar extension in quadruped. Flexion preference progression: progress from supine to standing forward flexion, add seated flexion. Neurodynamic sliders: e.g. for sciatic nerve — patient lies supine, gently flexes hip with knee extended and ankle dorsiflexion, then releases; perform in sets of 5-10 reps, 2-3 times daily, monitoring for peripheralization (if it peripheralizes, stop and regress). Core stabilization: dead bug (arms/legs), bird-dog, side-lying plank (regressed to modified plank), performed with attention to maintaining a neutral spine. Functional activity: graded sitting (start with 5-10 minutes, increase by 5 minutes every few days), standing, gentle bending/lifting with form cueing |
| Phase 3 | Progressive core and lumbopelvic strengthening; neurodynamic mobility (sliders → tensioners); functional training; graded return to provocative activities | Core strengthening progression: full plank, side plank, dead bug with resistance, bird-dog with resistance, anti-rotation drills (Pallof press). Neurodynamic tensioners (if sliders are well tolerated and no peripheralization): e.g. hamstring stretch with ankle dorsiflexion, holding at the point of tension for 30 seconds, repeated 3-5 times — only introduced once Phase 2 criteria met. Functional training: squat/lunge/deadlift patterns with postural cueing, loaded carrying (farmer's carry), lifting technique practice (moderate loads with perfect form). Endurance training: graded walking/hiking program, cycling (if flexion-tolerated). Sport-specific work: retraining golf swing, tennis serve, or other sport-specific postures with core stabilization cueing |

- **Centralization as the guiding principle:** if a movement or position causes the leg symptoms to retreat toward the spine (even if back pain temporarily increases), this is favorable and that direction/position should be incorporated into the exercise program. If peripheralization occurs, stop the provoking exercise immediately and reassess.
- **Pain-monitoring rule:** as in B8, exercise-related pain up to 3/10 NPRS that settles within an hour is acceptable. However, in B9, the location of pain is as important as the intensity — if a movement causes leg symptoms to worsen or move more distally (peripheralization), it should be avoided regardless of pain intensity. Document centralization/peripheralization at every visit.
- **Walking prescription:** Walking is the single most accessible early intervention. Prescribe: start with 5-10 minutes, 2-3 times daily, progressing by 5 minutes every few days as tolerated, aiming for 30-45 minutes daily. Monitor walking tolerance: if pain increases during walking, reduce duration or pace; if pain settles during walking, it's a good sign. Some patients with significant stenosis/irritability find walking aggravates symptoms — in these cases, use intermittent walking (short bursts with rest breaks) as a starting point.

> **Clinical Note on McKenzie Extension:** Repeated extension (prone press-ups) is the most common directional preference exercise for discogenic sciatica, as it encourages the herniated disc material to move anteriorly away from the nerve root (the "centralization" mechanism). However, not all patients centralize with extension — a subset centralize with flexion (particularly those with a more lateral herniation or foraminal stenosis). The clinical judgment is: test extension first, and if symptoms worsen/peripheralize, test flexion. The patient's response to these directional tests is the primary driver of Phase 1 exercise prescription.

### B9.8 Electrotherapy Detail

- **TENS:** Indicated for symptomatic pain relief in Phase 1, particularly for patients with high irritability or those who are not yet engaging effectively with active exercises due to leg pain. Conventional TENS (high-frequency, 80-120 Hz, low-intensity) applied to the lumbar paraspinal region and/or the referred leg pain area — teach the patient home-use TENS if night pain or prolonged sitting pain is a barrier to sleep/work function.
- **Heat pack:** Useful before manual therapy and exercise in Phase 1-2 to relax guarding and improve tissue extensibility, but avoid if it aggravates the radicular symptoms — some patients with a large herniation find heat increases inflammation and worsens pain; heat should be used cautiously and monitored for symptom response.
- **Ice:** If there is an acute inflammatory component (significant pain flare, swelling, severe irritability), ice applied to the lumbar region for 15-20 minutes, 2-3 times daily, may provide symptomatic relief in the first 24-48 hours. Use ice rather than heat if the patient is highly irritable.
- **Therapeutic ultrasound / IFT / Laser:** Weak evidence for discogenic sciatica specifically — may be used as an adjunct for secondary muscle pain/guarding if the clinic includes it, but never substitutes for directional preference exercise, manual therapy, or neurodynamic mobility.

### B9.9 Acupuncture / Dry Needling Detail

- Indicated for myofascial trigger points in the lumbar paraspinal muscles (erector spinae, multifidus, quadratus lumborum), gluteal muscles (gluteus medius, gluteus minimus), and piriformis, which are common in discogenic sciatica and contribute significantly to the secondary pain and guarding pattern.
- Particularly useful for trigger points in the quadratus lumborum (often painful and guarding on the affected side), gluteus medius (a common source of referral pain to the lateral hip and buttock), and piriformis (which can produce posterior hip and gluteal pain and may mimic or compound sciatica — though care is needed to distinguish true piriformis syndrome from sciatica).
- Rationale: reducing myofascial guarding can improve pain-free lumbar mobility, reduce referral symptoms, and allow more effective directional preference exercise and manual therapy in the same or following session — consistent with Module 2.5's acupuncture principle of enabling primary interventions.
- Not indicated as a primary treatment for the disc herniation itself — needling does not alter disc material, nerve root compression, or the chemical inflammatory cascade. It addresses the muscular component only, which is often secondary to the radicular pain.
- *(Full needle selection, depth, technique, and safety precautions for each lumbar/gluteal muscle will be detailed in Module 6: Acupuncture/Dry Needling Protocol Library.)*

### B9.10 Contraindications and Precautions

- **Cauda equina syndrome:** saddle anesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction, bilateral leg weakness, progressive neurological deficit — absolute contraindication to conservative care; immediate emergency referral (B9.12).
- **Progressive neurological deficit:** any worsening of motor weakness, sensory loss, or reflex change — requires urgent imaging and specialist referral, not continued conservative management.
- **Lumbar manipulation (high-velocity thrust):** Contraindicated in the acute phase of discogenic radiculopathy. In later phases (after radicular symptoms have substantially settled), manipulation may be considered by certified clinicians only, and only after a full safety screen. The risk of aggravating the herniation is significant; use Maitland mobilizations (Grade I-IV) as the primary manual therapy technique and avoid thrust manipulation if there is any residual radicular component.
- **Traction contraindications:** Do not use lumbar traction in patients with spinal fracture/instability, cauda equina, inflammatory spondyloarthritis (e.g. ankylosing spondylitis), or aortic aneurysm; use caution and lower forces in osteoporosis.
- **No imaging for routine sciatica without red flags:** MRI is indicated when: (a) severe or progressive neurological deficit is present, (b) red flags are positive (B9.12), (c) no improvement by Day 28 despite appropriate conservative care, or (d) surgical intervention is being considered. Avoid unnecessary MRI in the early acute phase if symptoms are mild/moderate and no red flags are present — it often demonstrates degenerative changes that are not the primary driver of the current symptoms.
- **Surgical referral indications:** persistent or worsening radicular symptoms with neurological deficit, cauda equina, spinal instability, or failure of conservative management (no meaningful improvement by Day 28) with a clear structural lesion on MRI — refer for orthopedic/neurosurgical opinion (B9.12).
- **Worst-case presentation:** a patient presenting with significant weakness (e.g. foot drop, significant quadriceps weakness affecting transfers) or a progressive history — consider earlier specialist referral in parallel with conservative management rather than waiting the full 28-day window, given the greater urgency of motor-dominant presentations.

### B9.11 Progression Criteria

Condition-specific thresholds, applied within the Module 2.7 generic framework:

**Progress to the next phase/loading level when:**

- Phase 1 → 2: Radicular pain is reducing in intensity and is centralizing; neurological exam is stable or improving (no new weakness, sensory loss, or reflex change); patient can correctly perform directional preference exercise without symptom exacerbation; walking program established; patient understands symptom-easing positioning.
- Phase 2 → 3: Leg symptoms have substantially resolved or are confined to the buttock/thigh (not below the knee); myotomal strength is improving toward full (if weakness was present); neurodynamic sliders are tolerated without peripheralization; functional mobility improved (sitting >20 minutes without significant pain, standing, bending with minimal discomfort).
- Within Phase 3, progress load/complexity when current exercise load is tolerated with ≤3/10 exercise pain that settles within 1 hour, no peripheralization, and no >24h flare.

**Regress or hold when:**

- Pain during exercise exceeds 3/10 or persists >1 hour post-exercise; or a >24h flare occurs (return to the prior tolerated load level).
- Peripheralization occurs (leg symptoms moving more distally) — stop the provoking exercise immediately and reassess; return to the prior tolerated phase and reintroduce progression more gradually.
- New or worsening motor weakness, sensory loss, or reflex change — halt progression, re-examine neurologically, and consider escalation per B9.12.
- Pain is centralizing (a good sign — reducing volume but not discontinuing).
- Pain is peripheralizing (a bad sign — stop the provoking exercise and reassess).

### B9.12 Red Flags Specific to This Condition

In addition to the universal red flags (Module 1, 1.2):

| Red Flag Category | Specific Indicators | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Cauda Equina Syndrome | Saddle anesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction, bilateral leg weakness, progressive neurological deficit, perianal sensory loss | Immediate emergency referral — do not perform any conservative treatment; patient requires urgent surgical assessment |
| Progressive Neurological Deficit | New or worsening motor weakness, sensory loss, or reflex changes — especially if bilateral or affecting bowel/bladder | Urgent referral for imaging and specialist assessment — do not continue conservative care if neurological status is worsening |
| Severe or Progressive Weakness | Significant weakness (e.g. foot drop, quadriceps weakness affecting transfers, or S1 weakness affecting gait) | Consider earlier specialist referral in parallel with conservative management — motor-dominant presentations have greater urgency |
| No Improvement by Day 28 | No meaningful improvement in radicular symptoms or neurological deficit despite appropriate conservative care | Refer for imaging (MRI) and surgical/orthopedic opinion — a subset of cases with significant compression do not resolve with conservative care alone |
| Saddle Anesthesia (any) | Any new perianal or perineal sensory loss, even without full cauda equina | Urgent referral — this is a red flag that may precede full cauda equina; do not delay |
| Bilateral Leg Symptoms | Bilateral radicular pain, weakness, or sensory loss (especially if progressive) | Urgent referral — suggests a large central disc herniation or cauda equina risk |
| Trauma or Significant Mechanism | High-velocity injury (MVC, fall from height) with sudden onset of severe back/leg pain | Urgent imaging — fracture or unstable injury must be ruled out before conservative management |
| Infection or Malignancy | Unexplained weight loss, fever/chills, night pain, history of malignancy, immunosuppression | Urgent medical referral — infection, malignancy, or other systemic cause must be ruled out |

### B9.13 Home Exercise Program

| Phase | Home program emphasis | Example content |
|---|---|---|
| Phase 1 | Directional preference exercise several times daily; symptom-easing positioning throughout the day; walking as tolerated; activity modification education | Extension preference: prone press-ups 5-10 reps, 3-5 times daily; standing extension; avoid sustained sitting and forward flexion; sidelying or supine with knees bent for symptom relief. Flexion preference: knee-to-chest 5-10 reps, 3-5 times daily; supine pelvic tilt; avoid sustained standing and extension. No clear preference: gentle cat-camel, pelvic tilts, walking; avoid sustained positions. "Take a break every 20-30 minutes" guidance; activity pacing |
| Phase 2 | Structured daily directional preference program; neurodynamic sliders; core stabilization; graded functional activity | Extension preference progression: press-ups with increased range/reps, standing extension. Flexion preference progression: standing forward flexion, seated flexion. Neurodynamic sliders: sciatic nerve slider (supine or sitting) 5-10 reps, 2-3 times daily — monitor for peripheralization. Core stabilization: dead bug, bird-dog, side-lying plank (modified), abdominal bracing during daily activities. Walking progression: increase by 5 minutes every few days |
| Phase 3 | Progressive home strengthening program; neurodynamic mobility (sliders → tensioners if tolerated); functional training; long-term relapse prevention | Core progression: full plank, side plank, Pallof press (if band available). Neurodynamic tensioners: hamstring stretch with ankle dorsiflexion (if tolerated). Functional training: squat/lunge/deadlift patterns with form cueing, loaded carrying. Endurance training: graded walking/hiking program. Sport-specific drills: golf swing, tennis serve, running mechanics with core cueing |

- **Most important patient education messages for this condition:**
  1. "The majority of disc herniations improve without surgery — your body has the capacity to absorb the herniated material over time. This takes weeks to months, not days."
  2. "Your symptoms may move around — that's normal. If the leg pain moves closer to your back, that's a good sign. If it moves further down your leg, that's a signal to slow down."
  3. "Do not stop moving completely — bed rest beyond 24-48 hours is harmful. Stay active within the limits of pain."
  4. "If you develop any new weakness in your leg, numbness in the saddle area, or bowel/bladder changes, contact us immediately — do not wait for your next appointment."
- **Flare management plan:** provide every patient with a written plan for managing future flares: (1) resume directional preference exercises; (2) use symptom-easing positions for comfort; (3) modify activities to avoid provocation; (4) use ice/heat/TENS for comfort; (5) if symptoms persist >48 hours or new neurological symptoms appear, contact the clinic immediately.
- **Address workplace ergonomics explicitly:** desk setup, chair with lumbar support, monitor height, regular breaks, lifting technique. Many patients have sedentary jobs and prolonged sitting is a major aggravator — optimize the workstation as a primary relapse prevention strategy.
- **Address sleep posture:** sidelying with a pillow between knees is generally best; supine with pillows under the knees is also good; avoid prone lying (which can extend the lumbar spine and aggravate some patients). Use a supportive mattress.
- **Address lifting technique:** teach "sit-to-stand" lifting (hinge at the hips, keep the back straight, engage the core, keep the load close to the body) — practice it with light loads in the clinic so the patient can do it safely at home.
- *(Full templated home program handouts will be built in Module 10: Home Exercise Program Templates.)*

### B9.14 Evidence Grade Summary

| Intervention | Evidence Level | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Directional preference exercise (McKenzie extension/flexion protocol) | Moderate-High | Strong evidence for acute lumbar radiculopathy; centralization is the key predictor of success |
| Exercise therapy (any form) | Moderate-High | Exercise is the primary treatment; directional preference approach is the most specific for this condition |
| Manual therapy (mobilization, not manipulation) + exercise combined | Moderate | Gentle mobilization as an adjunct to exercise, with radiculopathy-specific precautions; manipulation is contraindicated in the acute phase |
| Education and advice (staying active, "hurt ≠ harm" with radiculopathy-specific modifications) | Moderate | Essential component of care; emphasizes the favorable natural history and neurological monitoring |
| Neurodynamic mobilization (sliders → tensioners) | Moderate | Reasonable evidence for reducing neural mechanosensitivity; sliders are the safer starting point |
| Lumbar traction | Moderate | Specifically for radiculopathy; trial early and continue only if a reproducible benefit is seen |
| TENS | Low-Moderate | Symptomatic adjunct for pain modulation, especially for sleep disruption from radicular pain |
| Surgical discectomy/microdiscectomy | Moderate-High for the specific indicated subgroup | Reserved for progressive neurological deficit, cauda equina, or no improvement by Day 28 with a clear structural lesion |
| Corticosteroid injection (epidural) | Moderate | Considered by the referring physician for severe radicular pain not settling with conservative care — a medical decision, not physiotherapy-delivered |
| Dry needling (secondary myofascial guarding) | Low-Moderate | Adjunct only; addresses muscular component, not the nerve root compression itself |
| Therapeutic ultrasound / IFT / laser | Low | Weak adjunctive evidence; never a substitute for directional preference exercise or manual therapy |
| Bed rest | Harmful | Active rest (staying active within pain limits) is recommended; bed rest beyond 1-2 days delays recovery |

### B9.15 Outcome Measures & Cutoffs

| Measure | What it captures | Clinically meaningful change (MCID) | When to administer |
|---|---|---|---|
| ODI (Oswestry Disability Index) | LBP-specific disability | ~10-12 points | Baseline, then every reassessment point |
| RMDQ (Roland-Morris Disability Questionnaire) | LBP-specific disability | ~3-5 points | Baseline, then every reassessment point |
| PSFS (Patient-Specific Functional Scale) | Patient-defined functional goals | ~2 points | Baseline, then every reassessment point |
| NPRS — back and leg tracked separately | Pain intensity and centralization/peripheralization direction | ~2 points | Every session — track back and leg separately to monitor centralization |
| Myotomal strength (formal MMT grading) | Neurological status, progression monitoring | Any deterioration from baseline grade is clinically significant, not a percentage cutoff | Every visit until the radicular component is stable or improving |
| Sensory and Reflex Status | Neurological status, progression monitoring | Any new or worsening sensory loss or reflex change is clinically significant | Every visit until the radicular component is stable or improving |

### B9.16 AI Condition Card (RAG Metadata)

- **Condition:** Sciatica / Lumbar Disc Prolapse (Lumbar Radiculopathy)
- **Framework:** Standard 7-14-28 day phase framework, with centralization/peripheralization as the primary progression signal and neurological monitoring at every visit
- **Key Symptoms:** dermatomal pain radiating below the knee (L4, L5, or S1 distribution), positive SLR, myotomal weakness, dermatomal sensory loss, reflex changes, centralization/peripheralization with directional exercise
- **Red Flags:** cauda equina (saddle anesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction) — emergency; progressive neurological deficit; no improvement by Day 28; significant motor weakness (foot drop, quadriceps weakness affecting transfers)
- **Primary Treatment:** directional preference exercise (McKenzie extension in most patients, flexion in a subset), gentle manual therapy, neurodynamic mobilization (sliders → tensioners), core stabilization, education
- **Home Exercise Summary:** directional preference exercises several times daily and symptom-easing positioning (Phase 1) → structured directional preference program, neurodynamic sliders, core stabilization (Phase 2) → progressive strengthening, neurodynamic tensioners (if tolerated), functional training (Phase 3)
- **Typical Duration:** ~80-90% of cases improve with conservative management within 6-12 weeks; escalate for imaging/surgical opinion if no meaningful improvement by Day 28 or if neurological status worsens

*End of B9. Next in the tracker's work order: B10 — Low Back: Facet Joint Syndrome.*
